promptText: What is ChatModel in Spring AI, at its core?
options: A narrow, provider-agnostic Java interface with the shape ChatResponse call(Prompt prompt), implemented once per vendor
A concrete class that must be subclassed once per Spring Boot application
A configuration file format for describing prompts in YAML
A caching layer that sits between ChatClient and the Advisor chain
explanation: ChatModel is the thinnest possible seam between application code and a large language model — a Prompt goes in, a ChatResponse comes out, with vendor-specific translation handled entirely by the concrete implementation.

promptText: Does ChatModel maintain conversational memory internally, remembering what was said in a previous call?
options: Yes, every ChatModel bean keeps an internal session per caller automatically
No — ChatModel is stateless; every call is independent, and the caller must explicitly include all relevant prior messages in the Prompt on every call
Only when the provider is OpenAI; other providers require external memory always
Yes, but only for the duration of a single HTTP request
explanation: ChatModel is deliberately stateless, mirroring a well-designed stateless REST endpoint — conversational memory is a concern handled one layer up, by Advisors and ChatClient, never inside ChatModel itself.

promptText: Why does it matter whether an instruction is placed in a SystemMessage versus a UserMessage?
options: It doesn't matter at all — both are concatenated identically before being sent to the model

The model was trained with different statistical expectations for each role, so instructions placed in a SystemMessage are followed more reliably as standing behavioral constraints than the same instructions placed in a UserMessage
UserMessage content is encrypted before transmission while SystemMessage content is not
Only SystemMessage content counts toward the token budget
explanation: Mixing up roles doesn't throw a compile error and may even appear to work in casual testing, but it systematically weakens how reliably the model honors standing instructions once varied user input competes for its attention.

promptText: What kind of constraint is maxTokens on a ChatModel call?
options: A soft hint that the provider may ignore if it wants to give a more complete answer
A hard ceiling on how many tokens the model is allowed to generate, enforced by the provider and directly capping cost per request
The maximum number of input tokens the model can accept before rejecting the request
A client-side-only setting that has no effect on the actual provider call
explanation: maxTokens is a hard ceiling enforced by the provider on output tokens specifically; a response that hits this ceiling is truncated mid-structure with no exception thrown, which is different from an input-side context-window overflow.

promptText: What is the key difference between calling chatModel.call(prompt) and chatModel.stream(prompt)?
options: call() and stream() are identical; stream() is just a deprecated alias

call() blocks the calling thread until the entire response is generated and returns one ChatResponse; stream() returns a Flux<ChatResponse> emitting incremental partial chunks as they arrive, reducing perceived latency but not total generation time
stream() is only available for embedding models, never for chat models
call() always costs more tokens than stream() for the same prompt
explanation: Both terminate in the same ChatResponse type, but stream() delivers it incrementally via a reactive Flux, which is what powers visibly 'typing' chat UIs, while call() simply waits for the full result.

promptText: A ChatResponse holds a list of Generation objects rather than a single one. Why?
options: Because every call always returns exactly three candidate answers by default

To support providers that can return multiple candidate completions for the same prompt (e.g. a 'generate several options' feature); most calls only ever produce one Generation, accessed via getResult()
Because streaming responses are internally represented as a list of one Generation per token
Because Generation objects represent different providers' responses to the same prompt simultaneously
explanation: The type is honest about the possibility of multiple candidate replies (useful for 'generate N options' features) even though, absent that configuration, getResult() returning the first Generation is always correct and simpler.

promptText: A response comes back with finish reason "length" while your code is trying to parse it as JSON. What is actually happening, and whose responsibility is it to catch it?
options: ChatModel throws a JsonParseException automatically, so no extra code is needed

The maxTokens budget was hit mid-generation, producing syntactically incomplete text (e.g. JSON truncated mid-object) with no exception raised by ChatModel — it's the caller's responsibility to inspect the finish reason and decide whether to retry with a larger budget or reject the response
The provider automatically retries the call with double the token budget and returns the corrected result
This finish reason only ever occurs for streaming calls, never for blocking calls
explanation: A truncated response is returned as an ordinary, non-exceptional ChatResponse — silently trusting it as complete is a common source of intermittent downstream parsing failures unless the finish reason is checked explicitly.

promptText: Why is caching ChatModel responses keyed purely on prompt content risky once temperature is set above zero?
options: Because higher temperature calls are always rejected by the provider and never reach the cache layer

Because the same prompt can legitimately produce different, equally valid outputs on different calls at higher temperature, so a cache would serve one arbitrarily 'frozen' answer forever, semantically defeating the variability that was configured
Because temperature has no effect on output and caching is always safe regardless of its value
Because caching is only supported by Spring AI for embedding calls, never chat calls
explanation: At temperature near zero the output distribution is sharply peaked and close to deterministic, making prompt-keyed caching reasonable; at higher temperatures the same prompt validly yields different outputs, so caching becomes semantically wrong.

promptText: A feature needs OpenAI's frequency-penalty parameter, which has no equivalent in the neutral ChatOptions contract. What is the correct trade-off to make, per the chapter's guidance?
options: Never use provider-specific options under any circumstances; simulate the missing behavior entirely through prompt engineering instead

Reach for OpenAiChatOptions at that specific call site as a conscious, documented exception, accepting the resulting compile-time coupling to that provider's module, rather than defaulting to provider-specific options everywhere
Rewrite the neutral ChatOptions interface itself to add a frequency-penalty field usable by every provider
Switch the entire application to always use provider-specific options so all features stay consistent
explanation: The layered options model exists precisely so 90% of code stays portable while a feature can opt into the remaining 10% of provider-specific control explicitly, rather than the coupling being forced in implicitly or avoided entirely at the cost of quality.

promptText: In what order, from lowest to highest precedence, does Spring AI merge configuration for a ChatModel call?
options: Per-call ChatOptions, then application.yml auto-configured defaults, then framework defaults
Framework defaults, then application.yml auto-configured defaults (spring.ai.<provider>.chat.options.*), then any ChatOptions explicitly attached to that specific Prompt
All three sources are merged with equal precedence and the last one loaded wins arbitrarily
Only application.yml settings are ever used; per-call ChatOptions are ignored unless a bean is restarted
explanation: This mirrors how Spring resolves property sources generally: the more specific, closer-to-the-call-site value always wins, letting you set sensible application-wide defaults while still tuning an individual call.

promptText: What is the difference between a Prompt exceeding the model's context window and a response being truncated by maxTokens?
options: They are the same failure mode described with two different names

Exceeding the context window is an input-side problem where the provider rejects the request outright (surfaced as an exception); a maxTokens truncation is an output-side problem where the response is silently cut short with no exception at all
maxTokens truncation always throws an exception, while context-window overflow is always silent
Context-window overflow only happens during streaming calls; maxTokens truncation only happens during blocking calls
explanation: Context-window overflow is rejected up front by the provider and surfaces as an exception, while a maxTokens-truncated response looks like an ordinary successful ChatResponse and requires checking the finish reason to detect.

promptText: Why does depending on the ChatModel interface (rather than a concrete class like OpenAiChatModel) make unit testing dramatically simpler?
options: Because interfaces in Java run faster than concrete classes at test time

Because a plain Mockito mock of the interface can be stubbed to return a hand-built ChatResponse with zero network calls, no API key, and fully deterministic behavior, whereas the concrete class ties the test to provider-specific SDK types
Because ChatModel automatically generates test fixtures at compile time
Because only interfaces can be annotated with @Service in Spring
explanation: Because the service depends only on the interface, tests can mock it trivially and run in milliseconds — the model's own non-determinism never has to leak into the test suite at this layer.

promptText: When configuring a Resilience4j circuit breaker around a ChatModel bean, which failures should count toward tripping the breaker, and which should not?
options: All exceptions should count identically, since any failure indicates the provider is struggling

Transient failures (timeouts, 5xx responses, rate-limit errors) should count toward the failure-rate threshold; non-transient failures (invalid requests, bad credentials) should be excluded, since they indicate a code/config bug that won't be fixed by the circuit reopening later
Only rate-limit errors should ever be counted; all other failure types should be ignored by the breaker entirely
Non-transient failures should count double, since they are more severe than transient ones
explanation: A circuit breaker exists to stop hammering a provider that's genuinely struggling; counting non-transient failures (which will recur identically regardless of provider health) toward the same threshold would trip the breaker for the wrong reason and provide no actual recovery benefit.

promptText: A team runs a WebFlux application and calls the blocking chatModel.call() directly inside a reactive handler. Under moderate concurrent load, the application's throughput collapses even though CPU usage is low. What is the most likely cause, and what are the two standard fixes?
options: The provider is rate-limiting the application; the fix is to add a proactive token-bucket rate limiter

The blocking call is stalling WebFlux's small, fixed pool of event-loop threads for the entire multi-second generation duration, starving the pipeline; the fixes are to use the reactive stream() API end-to-end, or to explicitly offload the blocking call onto a bounded elastic scheduler
ChatModel beans are not thread-safe, so concurrent calls are corrupting shared state and must be synchronized
The JSON deserialization of ChatResponse is CPU-bound and should be moved to a virtual thread
explanation: WebFlux event-loop threads are meant never to block; a multi-second blocking call() parks one of the few available threads for its full duration, and a modest burst of concurrent requests can starve the whole reactive pipeline — the fix is to go fully reactive or explicitly move the blocking call to Schedulers.boundedElastic().

promptText: A production endpoint must return a fixed JSON schema and is seeing intermittent downstream JSON parse failures. Investigation shows the finish reason is occasionally "length," and separately, the team has enabled response caching keyed on prompt content with temperature set to 0.7 for variety. What are the two independent, correct fixes implied by the chapter's reasoning, without conflating them?
options: Lower maxTokens to save cost, and disable caching entirely for all endpoints regardless of temperature

Raise maxTokens with headroom for the JSON schema's worst-case size and monitor the 'length' finish-reason rate; separately, either drop temperature to near zero for this deterministic-extraction use case or stop caching this endpoint's responses, since caching a prompt at temperature 0.7 semantically freezes one arbitrary valid answer
Switch providers entirely, since any provider will silently truncate JSON output at any token budget
Increase temperature further to make the model less likely to produce incomplete JSON
explanation: These are two separate failure modes from the chapter: maxTokens truncation requires sizing the budget with headroom against the worst-case structured output and tracking the finish-reason rate as validation, while caching is only semantically sound near temperature zero — using it at temperature 0.7 for a task that wants variety serves one arbitrarily frozen answer forever, which is a distinct bug from the truncation issue.
